title: Sateesh Nori & Tom Martin — legal aid, Depositron, and 'access to justice, not access to lawyers'
pub: AAA 'AI and the Future of Law' podcast (hosts Bridget McCormack & Jen Leonard), YouTube
author: Sateesh Nori · Tom Martin

dom.t: Civil justice: Capacity gains need human safeguards

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: The source does not engage the cluster’s central concern that automation may erode apprenticeship and verification competence. Instead, it reframes legal technology as a liberating means to remove drudgery, restore community-facing practice and improve civil justice access.
qs: What’s the real harm in freeing yourself from the dry drudgery of legal work and getting back out into communities—being a small-town lawyer, hanging up a shingle, solving people’s everyday problems—and being able to make a living doing that with the proper tools and technology?
That’s what excites me: framing this as a positive, liberating moment for lawyers, not the destruction of the profession.

st.t: Legal software: Workflow layers defend specialist value
st.an: Nori does not assess whether legal-specific workflow layers defend specialist software value, nor does he provide evidence on AI copilots, verification or performance. Instead, he redirects attention to the access-to-justice problem and the need to rethink how legal help is delivered, offering motivation rather than a concrete technology proposition.
qs: This is not the best way to deliver help.
How can I think differently about access to justice?

st.t: Civil justice: Capacity gains need human safeguards
st.an: The source strongly supports expanding meaningful legal help beyond lawyer productivity and using AI to free lawyers for community-facing work. However, its aspiration to make legal aid obsolete through direct-to-public tools goes beyond—and potentially conflicts with—the cluster’s bounded-self-help framing, while offering limited discussion of human verification or evidence of legal outcomes.
qs: We talk about “access to justice,” not “access to lawyers.” What do we mean by justice?
Sateesh Nori: This is controversial given my background, but I want to make legal aid obsolete.We exist as legal aid because there’s a gap.

st.t: Justice augmentation: Activity exceeds proven access gains
st.an: The excerpt only introduces Nori and Martin as advocates for applying AI to the civil justice crisis. It provides no developed argument, implementation evidence, access outcomes, or view on preserving human relationships, so alignment with the cluster’s qualified proposition cannot be determined.
qs: Today we’re thrilled to be joined by two entrepreneurs, innovators, and advocates for using AI to address the civil justice crisis: Sateesh Nori and Tom Martin.

st.t: Reliable delivery: Legal engineering bridges capability and service
st.an: The host frames Nori and Martin as advocates for using AI to address the civil justice crisis and identifies relevant legal-aid and legal-technology experience. However, the excerpt contains no substantive remarks, evidence, or recommendations showing whether they endorse the cluster’s emphasis on multidisciplinary implementation, verification, task-specific evaluation, or reliable service delivery.
qs: Today we’re thrilled to be joined by two entrepreneurs, innovators, and advocates for using AI to address the civil justice crisis: Sateesh Nori and Tom Martin.
For 20 years, he represented tenants across New York City at various legal services organizations.

st.t: Service redesign: Resistance reflects incentives and identity
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s framing of AI as service redesign shaped by professional identity, and materially extends it with a concrete access-to-justice pathway beginning with problem recognition and proceeding toward triage and service delivery. Its claims remain largely aspirational and do not demonstrate measured outcomes or a complete implementation model.
qs: So it’s not surprising that our reaction to these tools is, “Nobody could ever replace us.” It’s so deeply ingrained in the culture that we’re the point of all this.
If you look at the line of legal service delivery, at the very beginning—the top of the funnel—the question is: Do I have a legal problem, and what does it mean?

st.t: Selective augmentation: Verification constrains uneven productivity gains
st.an: The source supports selective augmentation by presenting technology as a way to remove legal drudgery and restore lawyers’ community-facing work, while challenging the assumption that human legal work is error-free. Its claims about hallucination reduction and civil-justice impact are prospective and unvalidated, so it does not materially extend the cluster’s evidence on verification or productivity.
qs: What’s the real harm in freeing yourself from the dry drudgery of legal work and getting back out into communities—being a small-town lawyer, hanging up a shingle, solving people’s everyday problems—and being able to make a living doing that with the proper tools and technology?
Bridget McCormack: The double standard in how we evaluate human lawyering versus AI lawyering really gets under my skin.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: The source directly supports the proposition that AI can remove routine legal production without eliminating lawyers, framing automation as a way to redirect lawyers toward community-facing, human-centred work. Its access-to-justice and hallucination arguments are mainly aspirational and do not materially extend the cluster’s already broader account of bounded automation, verification and service-model change.
qs: What’s the real harm in freeing yourself from the dry drudgery of legal work and getting back out into communities—being a small-town lawyer, hanging up a shingle, solving people’s everyday problems—and being able to make a living doing that with the proper tools and technology?

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source supports selective, outcome-focused legal-AI deployment, especially for bounded access-to-justice uses. It treats AI as a potential complement or alternative where lawyer capacity is inadequate, while acknowledging that actual remedies require longitudinal evidence and institutional partnership. Its optimism and limited treatment of verification do not displace its overall alignment with the cluster’s cautious, use-specific proposition.
qs: We talk about “access to justice,” not “access to lawyers.” What do we mean by justice?
In terms of tracking long-term outcomes—how many people actually recovered their deposits—we don’t have full longitudinal tracking yet, but that’s in the works.

st.t: Workflow trust: Verification remains costly and contested
st.an: The source supports treating trust as a product of institutional safeguards rather than requiring error-free AI. McCormack points to tiered review as the legal system’s response to human fallibility and challenges rejection of AI merely because it hallucinates. Its access-to-justice and product claims are optimistic but prospective and provide no comparative performance or verification-cost evidence.
qs: We literally have a tiered system of review because judges get things wrong.
Bridget McCormack: The double standard in how we evaluate human lawyering versus AI lawyering really gets under my skin.

kp.k: AI offers alternatives to capacity-constrained, one-to-one legal aid
kp.d: Drawing on his legal aid experience, Nori argues that eligibility parameters, funding restrictions and daily turnaways limit traditional service delivery. He presents AI as a way to translate legal rules for ordinary people without relying solely on individual lawyers, freeing human resources for harder, higher-touch work. This is his proposed service model, not a measured productivity finding.
qs: We turn away people every single day. We have a narrow set of parameters for who we can help. We have grants, funders, and all kinds of limitations.
It’s no longer necessary to rely solely on individual lawyers to do that translation. We can do much more with less, and we can free up resources to focus on harder, higher-touch work.

kp.k: RAG connects conversational assistance to specified knowledge
kp.d: Martin explains retrieval-augmented generation as connecting a chatbot to a specific knowledge source, such as documents or written experience. Nori identifies seeing a RAG demonstration as a turning point in his approach to access to justice. Although McCormack asks about reducing or eliminating hallucinations, the discussion supplies no measured hallucination results.
qs: RAG stands for Retrieval-Augmented Generation.
you connect a chat interface—a chatbot—to a specific source of knowledge.
The chatbot can then refer to that information and intelligently answer questions based on it.

kp.k: Automation could redirect lawyers toward community problem-solving
kp.d: Nori argues that much existing legal work is screen-based research, email and paperwork rather than the human interaction lawyers anticipated. He frames AI as a potential release from routine work, enabling community-facing practice and earning a living solving everyday problems with appropriate technology, rather than necessarily destroying the profession.
qs: Now even the work you actually do is often something AI can handle much more easily.

What’s the real harm in freeing yourself from the dry drudgery of legal work and getting back out into communities—being a small-town lawyer, hanging up a shingle, solving people’s everyday problems—and being able to make a living doing that with the proper tools and technology?
That’s what excites me: framing this as a positive, liberating moment for lawyers, not the destruction of the profession.

kp.k: Law Answers requires explicit jurisdiction selection
kp.d: Martin describes Law Answers AI as nationwide legal information assistance intended to overcome lawyer availability and cost barriers. Users must select the relevant state, and he says answers are restricted to that jurisdiction rather than inferred from location. His favorable assessment of answer quality is experiential; no independent accuracy evaluation is reported.
qs: They try to get a lawyer on the phone, and it’s busy or it’s after hours. Even if they reach someone, it can cost hundreds of dollars.
When someone asks a question, the system requires them to define what state the question pertains to.
The system then answers based on that jurisdiction and only that jurisdiction.
I’ve seen a lot of lawyers on there asking questions, and the system holds its own.

kp.k: Depositron equips tenants to demand security deposit repayment
kp.d: Martin and Nori describe Depositron as giving tenants legally grounded language for demanding deposits back. Nori explains the proposed mechanism through legal citations, statutory penalties and photographs documenting apartment condition, which may persuade landlords to repay without a fight. This is a description of intended empowerment and dispute prevention, not established recovery effectiveness.
qs: People don’t always have the right words to ask for their deposit or demand it back. We give them those words. We give them a structured, legally grounded way to ask.
They don’t know how to leverage the penalties built into the law.
If they could transmit those photos, a landlord might decide to just give the money back, knowing the fight ahead isn’t worth it.

kp.k: Deposit market estimate relies on hypothetical improper withholding
kp.d: Nori estimates that about 200,000 people move annually in New York City, with an average security deposit of about $2,500, yielding $500 million. He then assumes 80 percent is returned or legitimately retained and describes the remaining 20 percent as a $100 million problem. The improper-withholding share is explicitly illustrative, not a reported measurement.
qs: In New York City, where I live, about 200,000 people move every year. The average security deposit is about $2,500.
200,000 times $2,500 is $500 million.
Say 80 percent of the time they give the money back or keep it for legitimate reasons, like damage to the apartment.
What’s 20 percent of $500 million? It’s a $100 million problem.

kp.k: Reported uptake differs; recovery outcomes remain untracked
kp.d: Nori says Depositron has helped thousands of New York City residents, whereas Martin later reports close to 700 interactions. The transcript does not reconcile those figures. Martin acknowledges that full longitudinal tracking of deposit recoveries is not yet available and says it is being developed; uptake therefore does not establish successful recoveries.
qs: Today, Depositron has helped thousands of people in New York City.
We’ve had close to 700 interactions with Depositron so far.
In terms of tracking long-term outcomes—how many people actually recovered their deposits—we don’t have full longitudinal tracking yet, but that’s in the works.

kp.k: Small collaborative teams can launch without institutional funding
kp.d: Nori reports that Martin built a prototype in weeks and that testing and launch occurred within months. Both advocate acting without waiting for grants or large nonprofit sponsorship. Martin presents collaboration across separate companies as a way to combine knowledge rather than treat organizational competition as a barrier.
qs: Incredibly, Tom built a prototype in weeks. We tested it and launched it within months.
You don’t need the Ford Foundation to back you. You don’t need a giant legal aid nonprofit to host you.
We each have knowledge to share, and we can bring it to a joint project.

kp.k: Expansion depends on awareness and state partnerships
kp.d: Martin says nationwide expansion is underway, with Illinois, Florida and California planned first. He identifies public awareness as an unresolved distribution challenge, credits launch news coverage with spreading awareness and plans to enlist state partners to amplify the service. These are rollout plans, not evidence of completed launches in those states.
qs: We’ll be launching in Illinois, Florida, and California—that’ll be the start.
If you build a better mousetrap but people don’t know about it, they won’t use it.
As we expand to new states, we’ll bring state partners into the loop and ask them to help amplify what we’re doing.

kp.k: Institutional resistance limits direct-to-consumer legal assistance
kp.d: Nori criticizes courts, legal aid organizations, governments and foundations for withholding support, attributing this partly to unauthorized-practice concerns, doubts about effectiveness and AI misconceptions. He estimates that security deposit disputes constitute something like 30 to 40 percent of small claims cases in the New York City context and argues that tools resolving them outside court could conserve resources. These are his characterizations and estimates, not institutional statements or documented caseload findings.
qs: In small claims court, which is where people go to fight for security deposits, something like 30 to 40 percent of cases are about that issue.
Instead, they’re wringing their hands about unauthorized practice of law and worrying, “Does it really work? What are we telling people?”
Even if we had a million-dollar marketing budget, the real challenge would still be changing minds in this space.

kp.k: Speakers challenge asymmetric standards for human and AI errors
kp.d: McCormack argues that human lawyers and judges make mistakes and that appellate review institutionalizes this recognition, while AI hallucinations are treated as disqualifying. Nori similarly acknowledges his own errors and suggests AI's Spanish-language capabilities could outperform his limited Spanish when assisting tenants. These are comparative arguments and examples, not measured demonstrations of safer AI legal advice.
qs: We literally have a tiered system of review because judges get things wrong. It’s a design feature.
But when an AI hallucinates, people say, “That’s it. It can’t possibly do what we lawyers do.”
There are things AI could do more reliably than I can.
So who’s actually providing better service there—me, or an AI with high-quality Spanish language capabilities?

kp.k: Justice should prioritize solutions rather than professional involvement
kp.d: Responding to reported critiques of AI as second-tier justice, Nori argues that people seek resolution of life problems rather than access to lawyers for its own sake. Martin invokes Cat Moon's client-centered approach and Richard Susskind's outcome-oriented analogy, arguing that AI help should be compared with the actual baseline of no assistance. McCormack separately invokes '92 percent of Americans who can’t afford a lawyer'; the transcript provides no supporting study for that figure.
qs: We talk about “access to justice,” not “access to lawyers.”
That doesn’t necessarily require a lawyer. People don’t care whether a lawyer is involved if their problem gets solved.
The before picture is: nothing. No help. “My landlord is keeping my money; what do I do?” The after picture is: you have some voice and some power to demand what’s yours.
Maybe we should ask the 92 percent of Americans who can’t afford a lawyer whether they’d like a free or low-cost solution.

kp.k: Lawyer-centered education reinforces resistance to alternative delivery
kp.d: Nori describes a mismatch between legal education's promises and actual legal work. Leonard recounts a design-thinking exercise in which portraits of lawyers and judges, rather than the public, prompted criticism of professional self-focus. She argues that this culture helps explain resistance to tools perceived as replacing lawyers; the evidence offered is anecdotal.
qs: There’s been a kind of bait and switch in legal education for a long time.
It’s strange that none of these pictures are of the public—the people you’re serving. It’s all lawyers.
From day one, everything is about us. So it’s not surprising that our reaction to these tools is, “Nobody could ever replace us.”

kp.k: Future ambitions span problem identification through resolution
kp.d: Martin's stated ambition is to scale assistance across identifying legal problems, triage and service delivery, including generating demand letters, helping send them and potentially tracking responses or offering court pointers. Nori's more expansive moonshot is to make legal aid obsolete by eliminating the access gap through direct, multilingual, always-available legal assistance. Both describe aspirations rather than demonstrated end-to-end resolution or achieved institutional replacement.
qs: That entire horizontal—from “Do I have a problem?” to resolution—is something many people are now trying to solve for.
We can generate that for you, help you send it, maybe even track the response and give pointers for court if you need that.
This is controversial given my background, but I want to make legal aid obsolete.
Ideas like Law Answers—the ability to search for an answer to any legal problem, from any perspective, in any language, at any time, from your phone—that’s how we liberate access to the law.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Nori and Martin describe AI as enabling scalable, direct-to-consumer legal help, reducing routine lawyer work and empowering people to resolve problems without necessarily obtaining a lawyer.
pts.d: Nori claims that AI can translate complicated legal rules for ordinary people, freeing lawyers for harder, higher-touch work. He presents this as professional liberation rather than destruction. Martin describes Depositron as giving tenants structured, legally grounded language to demand security deposits and Law Answers AI as making legal information available nationwide. Martin says Law Answers requires state selection and restricts answers to that jurisdiction. Nori suggests AI could perform some tasks more reliably than he can, using his own limited Spanish as an illustration. Both frame success around solving the user's problem rather than ensuring lawyer involvement. Martin's longer-term ambition extends from identifying legal problems through triage to document generation and resolution support. Nori's stated moonshot is to make legal aid obsolete by closing the access gap; this is an aspiration, not a reported outcome.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The speakers rely on professional experience, product-building experience, informal observations and usage figures; deposit-recovery outcomes are not yet fully tracked.
pts.d: Nori grounds the need for scalable services in two decades of tenant representation and legal aid's capacity and funding restrictions. He estimates a $100 million annual New York City deposit problem using approximately 200,000 moves and a $2,500 average deposit, then assuming 20 percent are improperly retained. That percentage is explicitly hypothetical; no supporting dataset is supplied. He reports a prototype built in weeks and launched within months. Nori says Depositron has helped thousands, whereas Martin reports close to 700 interactions; the transcript does not reconcile these figures or establish that interactions represent distinct users or successful recoveries. Martin explicitly acknowledges the absence of full longitudinal recovery tracking. His positive assessment of Law Answers rests on observing lawyers ask questions, not a reported benchmark or independent evaluation. Nori's Spanish comparison is illustrative rather than measured comparative evidence. No quantified reliability or hallucination-reduction results are supplied by the interviewees.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The interview distinguishes currently operating tools from undated expansion plans and broader aspirations; adoption depends on awareness, institutional support and jurisdiction-specific delivery.
pts.d: At the time of the 2025 interview, the speakers describe Depositron as launched in New York and Law Answers as available nationwide. Martin says expansion to Illinois, Florida and California is planned as the beginning of nationwide Depositron coverage, without dates. Law Answers' jurisdiction-specific operation depends on users selecting the relevant state rather than the system inferring location. Martin identifies public awareness as a condition of use and proposes state partners to amplify expansion. Nori identifies institutional resistance, including unauthorized-practice concerns and doubts about imperfect tools, as an obstacle even with substantial marketing funding. Martin's proposed end-to-end service includes possible response tracking and court pointers, not an assertion that all these capabilities are currently deployed. Nori's legal-aid-obsolescence ambition is conditional on reaching people directly and closing the access gap, with no forecast date.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal beneficiaries envisaged are underserved individuals, especially tenants; lawyers, legal aid providers and courts could also gain capacity.
pts.d: Martin describes tenants gaining a practical voice in deposit disputes and people unable to reach or afford lawyers gaining access to legal information. Nori's broader ambition includes multilingual, anytime access from a phone. Nori argues that direct-to-consumer tools can help people whom legal aid cannot serve, release lawyers from routine work, and support viable community-focused practice. He predicts courts would benefit if deposit disputes were resolved before filing, citing an unsourced estimate that roughly 30–40 percent of New York City small-claims cases concern deposits; no measured reduction in filings is presented. Landlords are affected as recipients of more legally grounded demands supported by evidence and potential statutory penalties. Nori also presents rapid, inexpensive development as an opportunity for innovators to address unmet needs without waiting for major foundations or large nonprofit hosts. These are civil access-to-justice claims, not claims about enterprise legal spending or large-firm staffing.
